name: Copper CRM
tagline: CRM platform native to Google Workspace ecosystem.
description: Copper CRM is a relationship manager built around Google Workspace, surfacing contact and deal context inside Gmail and Calendar.
pros: Contact, deal, and activity context appears beside the email already open, which removes the log-it-later step that sinks CRM adoption
Calendar entries carry the same relationship context, so meeting notes attach to records without re-entry
The object model stays deliberately small — leads, people, companies, deals — which keeps administration light for a team with no CRM owner
The paid band this dataset records, $23-69/mo, gives a buyer a starting figure before any vendor conversation
Teams already committed to Google Workspace get a CRM that behaves like part of that workspace rather than a neighbor application
cons: The Workspace assumption cuts both ways: an organization on Microsoft 365 is buying a design pointed somewhere else
High-volume dialing, sequenced outreach, and recorded-call analysis are not the product center, so outbound teams will add tools alongside it
This repository records no certifications or residency terms for Copper, and it does not itemize Copper's named connectors either

content.title: Copper CRM and the Google Workspace assumption
content.body: Copper CRM rests on an assumption most CRMs do not make: the sales team already works in Google Workspace, and the CRM should come to that work rather than the other way round. Contact records, deal context, and activity history surface inside the mail and calendar surfaces people already have open, so logging a conversation does not mean switching to a separate system of record. This repository files Copper under CRM & Sales with a paid model and a band of $23-69/mo, and its descriptor here is a CRM platform native to the Google Workspace ecosystem. Every capability below follows from that one placement decision.

content.title: Contact context where the email already is
content.body: The practical difference shows up in the daily loop. A new email arrives, the sender's organization, open deals, and recent activity appear beside it, and recording the touch does not require copying notes between tabs. Calendar events carry the same context, so a meeting note lands on the record it belongs to instead of in someone's memory. For a team that lives in a mailbox, this removes the step where CRM adoption usually fails — the part where people are expected to remember to update a second application. Copper keeps the record current by putting the record where the work already happens.

content.title: Pipeline, tasks, and reporting in Copper
content.body: Underneath the inbox layer sits a conventional CRM: leads and contacts alongside companies and deals, a pipeline board with stages, tasks assigned to owners, and reporting over pipeline and activity. Configuration is lighter than a suite CRM — fields and stages can be tailored to a sales process, but the product is not a platform for rebuilding a data model from scratch. That is the intended trade. This repository's CRM guide sorts the market along this axis, describing mid-market tools as focusing on pipeline management with interfaces sales teams adopt quickly, and Copper belongs on that side of the line rather than with the configurable suites.
items: Leads, people, and companies held as the core records
Deals tracked on a stage board with owners and values
Tasks and follow-ups attached to a contact or a deal
Saved views and filters that keep a rep's working list current
Pipeline and activity reporting for a manager's weekly review

content.title: What an inbox-first CRM does not cover
content.body: An inbox-shaped CRM has costs that follow from the shape. An organization running Microsoft 365 as its primary workspace is working against the design rather than with it. A sales motion built on high-volume dialing, multi-step sequenced outreach, or recorded-call analysis will not find those capabilities at the depth a dedicated engagement platform offers, because Copper's center is relationship context rather than outbound execution. And a team that wants deep custom objects, complex approval paths, or heavy cross-object reporting will meet the ceiling of a deliberately simple data model.

content.title: Connectors, API, and the data path
content.body: Copper's integration surface points at the Workspace relationship first: mail, calendar, and the file storage a sales team already uses, with an API covering anything outside that boundary. This repository does not enumerate Copper's named connectors, so specific pairings must be checked against the vendor's current listings. The security question lands in the same place: contact data flows through a Google-side workspace, which makes the data path part of the deployment decision, and no compliance certification, no retention schedule, no residency term, or identity control appears in the fields held here for Copper. Buyers handling regulated data should ask how much customer data leaves the Workspace boundary and under what terms.

content.title: Price record for Copper CRM
content.body: The stored price record for Copper CRM is a paid model with a band of $23-69/mo, and no free tier appears in these fields. The band does not indicate whether it is per seat, what the Workspace-side connectors cost, or which capabilities move to higher tiers, so it should be read as an entry reference rather than a quote. For scale, this repository's comparison records set the same field against Close CRM and Zoho CRM, each carried at its own recorded band. Confirm current list pricing and packaging with the vendor before budgeting.

content.title: Copper against Close, Pipedrive, and Zoho
content.body: Measured inside this dataset, Copper carries an overall score of 4.1/5 against Close CRM's 4.3/5, Zoho CRM's 4.2/5, Pipedrive's 4.4/5, and HubSpot's 4.5/5, with a band of $23-69/mo. Its nearest peers in the comparison records held here are Pipedrive, Zoho CRM, Close CRM, Salesloft, and Outreach — pipeline CRMs, a suite CRM, and two engagement platforms, none of which competes on Copper's specific ground of Workspace-native context.

content.title: Who Copper is built for
content.body: Copper is built for teams that run their day in Google Workspace and want relationship context attached to the mailbox rather than parked in another tab: small agencies, consultancies, and sales teams whose selling happens over email and scheduled meetings instead of cold calling. It is the wrong shape for organizations standardized on Microsoft 365, for high-volume outbound teams, and for buyers who need a highly configurable data model. What has been written here rests on Copper's own published documentation and on the fields this repository stores for the product.

faqs.question: Does Copper CRM require Google Workspace?
faqs.answer: It is designed around Workspace, so the mail-and-calendar context that defines the product targets teams on Google. This repository does not document non-Google behavior; confirm it with the vendor.

faqs.question: Is Copper a system of record or an inbox add-on?
faqs.answer: Both sides exist: contacts, companies, and deals live in Copper as the record, while the Workspace surfaces are where that record is read and updated during the day.

faqs.question: What price does this dataset record for Copper CRM?
faqs.answer: A paid model with a band of $23-69/mo and no free tier in these fields. Plan structure and tier boundaries are not captured, so treat the band as an entry reference.

faqs.question: How does Copper CRM differ from Close CRM?
faqs.answer: Close puts phone and email inside its own record and is built around calling; Copper puts the record inside Google's mail and calendar. Recorded band: $23-69/mo for Copper, with Close's carried higher in this dataset.

faqs.question: Are certifications recorded for Copper?
faqs.answer: No. Certification, retention, and residency fields are empty for Copper in this repository, so a security review has to start from the vendor’s own current documentation.

author: Sarah Chen
learningCurve: Inbox-driven daily use comes quickly; pipeline configuration, reporting, and connector setup take considerably longer.
whoShouldUse: Sales teams and consultancies that run their working day inside Google Workspace and want deals and history visible beside the email thread, especially where adoption depends on not introducing a second daily application.
whoShouldNotUse: Organizations standardized on Microsoft 365, high-volume outbound teams that need dialing and sequences at depth, and buyers who require extensive custom objects or certification evidence this dataset does not hold.
